fact_text: Any adult aged 18 or over is generally liable for Council Tax on the property they occupy. A full Council Tax bill assumes at least two adults in the home; spouses and partners living together are jointly and severally liable.
evidence_quote: You'll usually have to pay Council Tax if you're 18 or over. A full Council Tax bill is based on at least 2 adults living in a home. Spouses and partners who live together are jointly responsible for paying the bill.

fact_text: A 25% discount applies if the resident lives alone, or if all other occupants in the property are legally 'disregarded'. The discount must be claimed from the local council — it is not applied automatically.
evidence_quote: You'll get 25% off your bill if you pay Council Tax and either: you live on your own; everyone else in your home is disregarded

fact_text: If every occupant in a household is 'disregarded' (e.g. all full-time students), the discount rises to 50%. An exemption or discount application must still be submitted to the local council even when all occupants are disregarded.
evidence_quote: You'll get 50% off your bill if everyone living in your household is disregarded. … Apply for a Council Tax discount or an exemption, even if you're disregarded.

fact_text: Council Tax is calculated by reference to a valuation band (A–H in England and Wales) assigned to the property by the Valuation Office Agency, based on estimated property value in April 1991. The annual amount for each band is set by each local council individually — confirm the current figure at review with your local council.
evidence_quote: You'll need to know 3 things: the valuation band for your home in England and Wales or in Scotland; how much your local council charges for that band; whether you can get a discount or exemption from the full bill

fact_text: A household where every occupant is a qualifying full-time student owes no Council Tax at all. If a bill is received, an exemption must be applied for from the local council. If only some occupants are students, the household may still qualify for a partial discount.
evidence_quote: Households where everyone's a full-time student do not have to pay Council Tax. If you do get a bill, you can apply for an exemption. … You'll get a Council Tax bill if there's someone in your household who's not a full-time student, but your household might still qualify for a discount.

fact_text: To count as a 'full-time student' for Council Tax purposes, the course must last at least one year and involve at least 21 hours of study per week. For a qualification up to A-level taken by a student under 20, the course must last at least 3 months and involve at least 12 hours of study per week.
evidence_quote: To count as a full-time student, your course must: last at least 1 year; involve at least 21 hours study per week. If you study for a qualification up to A level and you're under 20, your course must: last at least 3 months; involve at least 12 hours study per week

fact_text: All state school applications in England are routed through the local council (local authority), whether for schools in the family's own area or in another council's area. Contacting the local council is the mandatory first step for any state school place.
evidence_quote: If you live in England contact your local council to find: state-funded schools in your area; admission criteria for the schools you're interested in

fact_text: Families relocating from another country must contact the local council in the area where they will be living in England to apply for a state school place. They may be required to supply proof of their new UK address and demonstrate they will be living there before the start of the next school term.
evidence_quote: If you're applying from another country, contact the local council in the area where you're going to live. You may need to: supply proof of your new address, for example a mortgage or rental agreement or deeds for the property; prove that you'll live in the area before the start of the next school term

fact_text: Families arriving mid-year must apply through the in-year admissions process. They contact their local council, which identifies schools with available places and advises on how to apply. Once a place is offered, the child typically starts at the beginning of the following term.
evidence_quote: Contact your local council to find out about applying for a school place once the school year has started (known as in-year applications). They can tell you which schools still have places and how to apply. Once your child has been offered a place, they will usually start school at the beginning of the following term.

fact_text: If no school place is immediately available, the family can place the child on a waiting list. The admission authority (usually the school or the council) is legally required to keep a waiting list open for at least the first term of each school year. A child may be on a waiting list even while already attending another school.
evidence_quote: The 'admission authority' for the school (usually the school itself or the council) must keep a waiting list open for at least the first term of each school year. … You can add your child's name to a waiting list even if they have been offered a place at another school.

fact_text: The local council has a legal duty to provide a school place even if the child is not offered a place at any of the preferred schools applied for. This will usually be the nearest school with places still available.
evidence_quote: The local council must provide a place at another school, if your child is not offered a place at any of the schools you've applied for. This is usually your nearest school with places still available.

fact_text: India is not on the DVLA designated-country exchange list. An Indian driving licence holder cannot exchange their licence directly for a GB licence. They must pass the full GB driving test (theory and practical) to obtain a GB licence.
evidence_quote: Foreign drivers must prove they have passed an appropriate driving test before getting a British licence under tough new rules … requests to exchange driving licences from outside the EU will only be accepted if the licence holder can prove they passed a driving test in a country where the testing standards are comparable with those in Britain. … DVLA also has reciprocal arrangements in place for the following countries: Australia, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Canada, Falkland Islands, Faroe Islands, Hong Kong, Japan, Monaco, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Singapore, South Africa, Switzerland, Zimbabwe [India is not listed]

fact_text: A person holding a valid non-UK, non-EEA driving licence who becomes resident in Great Britain may drive on that foreign licence for up to 12 months from the date they become resident. After 12 months of GB residency, they must either exchange their licence (if from a designated country) or pass a GB driving test. India is not a designated country, so Indian licence holders must pass the full GB test after 12 months.
evidence_quote: In Great Britain, we allow all those driving on non-UK, non-EEA driving licences who become resident, 12 months before we require them either to exchange their licences if eligible, or to take a driving test in order to continue driving here.

fact_text: A second official gov.uk source independently confirms that after 12 months of UK residency, a foreign licence holder must exchange or replace their licence to continue driving in the UK. This is stated in the e-scooter trial user guidance published by the Department for Transport.
evidence_quote: If you have been resident in the UK for more than 12 months, you must exchange your licence if you wish to continue driving in the UK.

fact_text: As of the 2013 press release, the non-EU/EEA countries with GB driving licence exchange agreements were: Andorra, Australia, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Canada, Falkland Islands, Faroe Islands, Hong Kong, Japan, Monaco, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Singapore, South Africa, Switzerland, Zimbabwe — plus all EU and EEA states. India is not on this list. Confirm the current designated-country list at review via the DVLA exchange tool at gov.uk/exchange-nongb-driving-licence, as the list can be updated by secondary legislation.
evidence_quote: DVLA also has reciprocal arrangements in place for the following countries: Australia, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Canada, Falkland Islands, Faroe Islands, Hong Kong, Japan, Monaco, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Singapore, South Africa, Switzerland, Zimbabwe

fact_text: Banks require proof of address to open a UK account. Proof of address is defined as an official letter showing the applicant's name and current UK address — for example, a letter from a government body or from a utility company.
evidence_quote: Proof of address is usually an official letter which shows your name and your current address (for example, from the government, or a utility company).

fact_text: For a new arrival from outside the EEA, banks accept the following identity documents: a Biometric Residence Permit (BRP), a valid national passport, and the official letter from the British government granting permission to stay in the UK (e.g. visa approval letter).
evidence_quote: your identification and visa documents, which can include: Biometric Residence permit; your [national] passport; the letter you received from the British government allowing you to stay in the UK

fact_text: If a new arrival does not yet have a UK proof of address, some banks offer an alternative verification method — for example, a host or guarantor attending a branch in person with their own ID and proof of address. The specific alternatives accepted vary by bank; applicants should check with the individual bank before visiting.
evidence_quote: If you don't have a proof of address some banks will allow you to bring your host along to verify where you live (they will need to show their ID and proof of address). Check the bank's website to find out what they will accept before you apply.

fact_text: A 'basic bank account' is a fee-free fallback account for those who cannot open a standard account. It allows receipt of salary and benefit payments at no charge. Some banks offer basic accounts on direct application; others only offer them to applicants who are ineligible for their standard accounts. Applicants should ask explicitly.
evidence_quote: A basic bank account doesn't charge any fees for using it. You can receive your salary or money from benefits, with no charge. Some banks and building societies let you apply directly for a basic bank account, and others only offer basic bank accounts to customers who are not eligible for their other accounts.

fact_text: A UK bank or building society account can be opened in person at a branch (possibly by appointment), by phone, online, or via a bank's mobile app. If applying in branch, identity documents must be brought. Official guidance states that banks and building societies should consider alternative ways to identify and verify customers — meaning a new arrival without the standard documents should still attempt to apply.
evidence_quote: You can apply for an account by: going to a bank or building society branch (you may need to make an appointment); by phone; online; a bank's mobile app. … Banks and building societies should consider other ways to identify and verify their customers.
